issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction of a tenant from a non-residential building for business use must plead and prove the statutory conditions for that ground of eviction.
material_facts: The landlords sought eviction under section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, to start a readymade-garment business in the shop.

The eviction petition pleaded the bona fide business requirement but did not plead that the landlords were not occupying another non-residential building of their own or one to whose possession they were entitled.
The landlords disclosed other non-residential buildings owned by one landlord, and the evidence showed those buildings were occupied by tenants.
issues.conclusion: The conditions in section 10(3)(a)(iii) must be pleaded in the eviction petition and proved at trial; proof without appropriate pleading is generally irrelevant.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, a landlord seeking a non-residential building for an existing or proposed business must plead and establish the bona fide business requirement and that the landlord has no other qualifying non-residential accommodation. The Court adopted the pleading principle stated in Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, [1981] 3 SCR 605, including that proof without appropriate pleading is generally of no relevance.

predicates.nonresidential_business_eviction: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding concerning a non-residential building.
predicates.landlord_seeks_business_use: The landlord seeks the building to continue or commence a business.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_condition_appl: The ground for eviction makes the landlord's lack of qualifying alternative non-residential accommodation a condition of relief.
predicates.landlord_must_plead_and_prove_business_n: The landlord must plead and prove the bona fide business need and the lack of qualifying alternative non-residential accommodation.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks a non-residential building for business use under a ground that requires the landlord to lack qualifying alternative accommodation, the landlord must plead and prove both the business need and that lack.

issues.legal_issue: An eviction order need not be set aside for an omission in the eviction pleading when the objection is raised for the first time on final appeal, the material is already on record, and no further evidence is identified that could affect entitlement to eviction.
material_facts: The tenant did not raise the pleading omission before the Rent Controller, the appellate authority, or the High Court, and did not include it in the special leave petition; the objection was raised for the first time in argument before the Supreme Court.
The landlords disclosed the other non-residential buildings owned by one landlord, and those buildings were occupied by tenants.
The landlords gave reasons for selecting the disputed shop for the proposed business, including its central business location and the presence of other readymade-garment shops nearby.
The tenant did not claim that further evidence after amendment of the pleadings could show that the landlords occupied suitable alternative accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the eviction order because the pleading objection was raised for the first time at that stage and, on the record and submissions, remand would be futile.
issues.legal_principle: Although the conditions in section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, must be pleaded and proved, the Court found no justification to interfere where the omission was not raised in the lower courts or in the special leave petition, the relevant materials were already on record, and the tenant identified no further evidence that could affect the landlords' entitlement. The Court applied the pleading principle from Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, [1981] 3 SCR 605, but dismissed the appeal on the circumstances of this case.

rule.if: appeal_from_eviction_order and pleading_objection_raised_first_time_on_final_appeal and relevant_material_already_on_record and no_further_evidence_claimed and alternative_buildings_disclosed_as_tenant_occupied

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_order: A tenant appeals from an order directing eviction.
predicates.pleading_objection_raised_first_time_on_: The tenant first objects to a pleading omission during the final appeal, without raising it in the earlier proceedings or the appeal papers.
predicates.relevant_material_already_on_record: The materials relevant to the omitted pleading issue are already before the court.
predicates.no_further_evidence_claimed: The tenant does not identify further evidence that could affect the landlord's entitlement to eviction.
predicates.alternative_buildings_disclosed_as_tenan: The landlord disclosed other owned non-residential buildings, and those buildings were occupied by tenants.
predicates.eviction_order_not_set_aside_for_late_pl: The eviction order is not set aside on the basis of the late-raised pleading objection.

issues.definition: When a tenant appeals an eviction order, first raises a pleading objection at the final appeal, and the relevant record is complete without a claim of consequential further evidence, disclosure that other buildings are tenant-occupied supports leaving the eviction order undisturbed.
